idiom_name: endpoint authorization policies plus IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync for point-of-use decisions
implementation_notes: ASP.NET Core supplies the always-invoked half: the authorization middleware evaluates an endpoint's policies on every request ([Authorize(Policy = ...)] or RequireAuthorization), and resource-based authorization is the documented point-of-use form - AuthorizeAsync(user, resource, policy) once the resource has been loaded, because the earlier pipeline check could not see it. The platform's classic in-process monitor has been retired: Code Access Security, which demanded permissions and walked the call stack to catch luring attacks, is documented as not supported in .NET Core and .NET 5+ and explicitly not to be used as a security boundary. The small verifiable core is therefore what you write: a sealed class registered in DI whose single decision method takes the principal and the operation, reads a replaceable policy store, and fails closed on a missing identity or an unreachable store, covered by its own table-driven test suite.
pitfalls: Endpoints that never received a policy are anonymous by default: minimal-API routes without RequireAuthorization, or with AllowAnonymous, are not mediated at all, so the route-to-policy enumeration is part of the verification.
DI lifetimes redraw the trust boundary: a singleton monitor that keeps per-request state leaks decisions between users, and a cached AuthorizationResult outlives revocation.
Reflection and InternalsVisibleTo reach internal or private members of the monitor, and the CLR no longer offers an in-process sandbox - the sealed class is reviewable, not tamperproof.

A custom IAuthorizationHandler that calls context.Succeed(requirement) on a path it does not really evaluate turns the monitor into a rubber stamp; handlers must fail closed and be tested with a principal that must be denied.
